context: Current closing price of Johnson & Johnson (JNJ): $234.34 USD as of 2026-05-25.
justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what appears to be a current price level around $234–235, with very little directional conviction at any horizon. At the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the current price with only a slight positive bias, reflecting the general tendency of equity or asset prices to drift marginally upward in the absence of strong catalysts. At the one-week horizon, I maintained nearly the same point estimate, acknowledging that short-term mean reversion and noise tend to dominate over such brief windows, making large directional moves unlikely in expectation. At the one-month horizon, I allowed for slightly more upward drift, consistent with a modest positive drift assumption, but the estimate itself remains close to the current level because a single month is too short for fundamental trends to assert themselves strongly.

The confidence interval widths expand meaningfully as the horizon lengthens, which reflects the standard square-root-of-time scaling of uncertainty in financial markets. At one day, the interval is quite tight at plus or minus roughly five points, consistent with typical daily volatility for a mid-priced asset. By one week, I widened it to reflect that multiple daily moves can compound in the same direction, and by one month, the interval spans roughly 36 points in total, acknowledging that a full month of trading sessions can produce substantial cumulative movement. The width also reflects my uncertainty about the underlying volatility regime itself — whether conditions are calm or stressed matters enormously.

There are several specific risks that could push outcomes well outside my stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden deterioration in macroeconomic data, an unexpected central bank policy shift, geopolitical escalation, or a credit event in a systemically important institution could trigger sharp selling that breaches the lower bound, particularly at the one-month horizon. On the upside, stronger-than-expected earnings, a dovish policy surprise, or a broad risk-on sentiment shift could push prices above my upper bounds.

It is worth noting that my intervals implicitly assume relatively normal market conditions. Fat-tail events — the kind that appear in financial markets far more frequently than a Gaussian distribution would suggest — are not fully captured by my stated confidence bounds. A true black swan event, whether a sudden liquidity crisis or an exogenous shock, could produce moves that dwarf even my one-month interval. Readers should treat these estimates as a central tendency with moderate uncertainty, not as hard boundaries on what is possible.
